extracted.intended_audience: writers, playwrights, actors, and literate readers interested in prose/style and theatrical criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance and criticism for writing and staging (prose, essays, comedy, and theatre), emphasizing clarity, appropriateness of subject and manner, and moral/esthetic judgement. Includes points about public reputation/glory and models of sincere love in letters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive circumstantial detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not let a speaker or writer ramble into minute, irrelevant particulars (settling the geography of a jest, exact time and place) that add nothing to the point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the narrator leaves a man who 'plays away its Words, with uttering nothing to the Purpose' — such circumstantiality wastes readers' time. Be economical: don't substitute tedious exactness for meaningful content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't over-rely on authorities to pad argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using citations of famous authors merely to lend weight to trivial or self-evident claims; do not substitute heavy quotation/reading for your own judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: a preacher 'proving out of these great Authors Things which no Man living would have denied him' and prefacing remarks with long references (folio, page numbers). Such practice strains modesty and weakens original engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pedantic disputation and frivolous scepticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not raise needless doubts about plain matters or force disputes where there is no controversy; frivolous questioning turns knowledge into unanswerable hair-splitting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Antipatterns: insisting about what time someone was seen, or arguing 'Snow is white' into metaphysical claims that there is no colour in nature. Such talent makes one always frivolous and unanswerable rather than useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acting must be exact, proper, and graceful
rubrics_metrics.description: On stage, performers must be exact and graceful — mere bare performance is not commendable and the slightest error is contemptible because theatrical pleasure depends on precision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the audience expects only the pleasures of ears and eyes, 'the least Diminution of that Pleasure is the highest Offence.' Physical awkwardness or lack of propriety reduces theatrical effectiveness; weight of matter can excuse some defects in other public speaking but not in theatrical performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep spectacle (corporeal feats) separate from intellectual acting
rubrics_metrics.description: Bodily feats (rope-dancing, tumbling, dangerous acrobatics) should not be mixed with performances that require representation of passions and ideas; separate the bear-garden from the stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposal: dismiss corporeal actors to places suited for spectacle, reserving the main stage for actors who can represent passions and intellect. Mixing these confuses genre and lowers quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match subject matter to dramatic genre appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjects that are dark, horrid, or bloody (e.g., witchcraft) belong to tragedy or serious drama where they are integral; such material is foreign to comedy unless transformed by extraordinary imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Macbeth's witches are suitable because they are part of the tragic story and handled with solemnity; inserting similar material in comedy produces incongruity and fails to entertain unless mediated by genius (e.g., Shakespeare).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not pander to the lowest tastes; respect modesty
rubrics_metrics.description: Playwrights and writers should avoid coarse, indecent jests that may raise loud mirth but are painful to right sense, and should not sacrifice the best part of their audience to the worst.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism of plays that include liberties offensive to modesty: such jests may please 'orange-wenches' but disgrace the boxes. Aim to please 'People of the best Understanding.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure moral endings are fitting and not facile excuses
rubrics_metrics.description: A play's or story's moral resolution should not trivialize or excuse wrongdoing with empty philosophy ('Design whate'er we will, There is a Fate which over-rules us still') — moral treatment must be appropriate to the actions represented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Antipattern: ending by suggesting fate absolves characters of responsibility; such conclusions can be thinly veiled rationalisations that undermine moral seriousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer the just, proper, and natural in prose over forced wit
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid imitating certain 'beauties' (antique/uncouth words, quaint antithesis, forced allusion, point-turns) that prioritize cleverness over correctness and naturalness; aim for what is just, proper and natural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of imitators of Milton, Cowley, Ovid: focusing on 'point' or 'turn' and odd diction produces affected writing. Such luxuries are called 'Blemishes' and mistaken for genuine wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance learning with accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not be so 'nice' or so learned that readers cannot understand you; maintain clarity and avoid excessive erudition that makes prose impenetrable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers complain 'you are often so Nice there is no enduring you, and so Learned there is no understanding you.' Good writing communicates; adjust learning to audience comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfection of glory (Tully's three elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: A formula for evaluating public greatness: the people love us; they have confidence in us; and they think we deserve honour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to princes and public figures: to assess 'glory', check for popular affection, trust/confidence, and a general sense of deserving honour. For a favourite under a prince, add reciprocal favour as necessary for durable glory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of truly glorious leadership (depiction guideline)
rubrics_metrics.description: True glory in a prince/leader arises from personal labour, personal knowledge, modesty, and the use of power to improve people's arts and lives — not from ostentation or vanity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Peter of Russia learned crafts, travelled incognito to study arts of peace and war, joined the army as a private to set an example. Such personal application lays foundation for lasting fame; avoid depicting greatness as mere pomp or conquest without public betterment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayals of love should emphasize steady virtue over romantic theatrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Authentic representations of love in letters and fiction favor constancy, piety, mutual respect, modesty, and lifelong devotion rather than 'romantick' whining and theatrics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by preserved love-letters showing prayerful, steady affection and improvement of character; writers should model love as Christian, honourable, and disinterested to create respectable sentiment.
